carFuel.faq.1.q: Why are there two break-even figures?
carFuel.faq.1.a: Without interest, break-even is when the fuel saved equals the extra price. With interest, the extra price also grows at your loan rate, because that money was borrowed or could have earned elsewhere. The second figure comes later, and the verdict uses it.
carFuel.faq.2.q: Where do the fuel prices come from?
carFuel.faq.2.a: Choose your city under Assumptions. Verified city prices fill in automatically, with their source and date in the table above. Prices change daily, so check your local pump.
carFuel.faq.3.q: Does it include resale value, insurance or kit servicing?
carFuel.faq.3.a: Yes, if you enter them. Under “Insurance, resale and one-off costs” you can add each car's yearly insurance, what it sells for at the end, and a one-off cost such as a cylinder or battery replacement. Left empty, they are treated as the same for both cars. Add other yearly running costs, such as cylinder testing or kit servicing, under Extra upkeep.
carFuel.faq.4.q: What if I drive less than the example?
carFuel.faq.4.a: The saving shrinks with distance. “What would flip the answer” shows the monthly distance below which petrol wins with your numbers.

solar.metaDescription: Rooftop solar payback with your own bill: payback year, savings over 25 years and yearly return, with every assumption shown.
solar.explanation: Each month, the panels generate system size × generation per kW per day × 365 ÷ 12 units, less a little each year as they age. Your bill is worked out twice: on all the units you use, and on only the units you still buy from the grid, minus credit for any units you send to it. The difference is the saving. Because the bill uses the tariff's slabs, the units you save come off the most expensive slab first. Payback is the month when savings cover the price after subsidy. In Delhi, both bills also go through the government subsidy if you have opted in, so solar saves only what you would still pay.
solar.faq.1.a: Subsidy, generation, panel loss and export credit depend on rules and data we have not verified yet, so we do not guess them. Enter the figures from your installer's quote and your bill.
solar.faq.2.q: Why does it ask for an average price per unit in UP?
solar.faq.2.a: For Delhi the tool uses the DERC tariff, with its subsidy if you have opted in. For UP, until its slab tariff is verified, it uses one price for every unit plus your fixed charge: divide your energy charge and duty by the units on your bill.
solar.faq.3.a: The interest rate at which the money you put into the system would grow to the same savings. Compare it with what the money would earn elsewhere, after tax.

rentBuy.metaDescription: Rent or buy a home, with your own numbers: net worth of each path after the years you choose, when buying overtakes renting, and the home price growth it needs.
rentBuy.explanation: The tool follows two households month by month. The buyer pays the EMI, maintenance and property tax. The renter pays rent and invests what the buyer spent at purchase. Each month, whoever pays less invests the difference at your return. At the end, the buyer's net worth is the home's value less the loan still owed and the cost of selling, plus anything they invested; the renter's is their investments plus the deposit back.
rentBuy.faq.1.a: Because the renter invests the down payment and stamp duty instead of spending them, and keeps investing whenever rent is cheaper than owning. If your return beats home price growth after costs, renting and investing can end ahead.
rentBuy.faq.2.a: Not yet. They depend on your tax regime and the current rules, which we have not verified. Leaving them out makes buying look slightly worse than it may be under the old regime.
rentBuy.faq.3.a: What the renter's money would actually earn after tax, in whatever they would really invest it in. A lower figure favours buying; a higher one favours renting.

page.methodology.title: How we work out the numbers
page.methodology.description: The formulas behind every CapitalVerdict calculator, in plain language: monthly simulation, EMI, break-even, scenarios, what flips the answer, and today's rupees.
page.methodology.intro: Every tool runs the same way: a month-by-month simulation of each option, using only the figures you can see and change on the page. This page sets out the rules they share and the formula behind each tool. The code that does the maths is tested against numbers worked out by hand.
page.methodology.conventions.title: Rules every tool follows
page.methodology.conventions.body:
Time moves in months. A tool starts at month 0, the day you decide, and steps forward one month at a time to the end of the period you choose.

Prices that rise each year (fuel, electricity, rent) stay flat for twelve months and then step up by the yearly rate. Investment returns and home prices grow a little every month, at the monthly rate that adds up to the yearly figure you enter.

Nothing is rounded until it is displayed.
page.methodology.conventions.formula:
monthly rate     = (1 + yearly rate)^(1/12) − 1
price in year y  = starting price × (1 + yearly rise)^(y − 1)
page.methodology.loan.title: Loans and EMI
page.methodology.loan.body: Loan rates are quoted the way banks quote them: a yearly rate divided by 12 for each month. The EMI is the fixed monthly payment that clears the loan exactly at the end of the tenure. Each month, interest is charged on what is still owed and the rest of the EMI repays the loan.
page.methodology.loan.formula:
r   = yearly rate ÷ 12
n   = tenure in months
EMI = loan × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1)
page.methodology.breakeven.title: Break-even
page.methodology.breakeven.body: Break-even is the first month in which the running total of what an option saves catches up with what it cost upfront. If that never happens within the period you chose, the tool says so instead of guessing beyond it.
page.methodology.scenarios.title: Scenarios and what flips the answer
page.methodology.scenarios.body:
The pessimistic, base and optimistic results rerun the same calculation with the values in the default scenario table, changing only the inputs the table covers. They are a range of reasonable assumptions, not forecasts.

"What would flip the answer" changes one input at a time and holds everything else. It searches for the value at which the result crosses zero, which is where the other option starts to win.
page.methodology.todaysRupees.title: Today's rupees
page.methodology.todaysRupees.body: A lakh in fifteen years buys less than a lakh today. Where a tool shows an amount in today's rupees, it divides the future amount by inflation over the same period.
page.methodology.carFuel.title: Petrol, CNG or EV
page.methodology.carFuel.body:
For each car, the monthly running cost is the fuel or electricity for your distance plus a twelfth of the yearly upkeep. The saving is the petrol car's cost minus the other car's.

The extra purchase price is charged interest at the rate you enter, because that money is either borrowed or not invested. Break-even is the month the running total of savings reaches the extra price with interest added. The savings themselves are not assumed to be invested.

For an EV, the price per unit blends home and public charging by the share you charge at home.
page.methodology.carFuel.formula:
monthly cost   = km a month ÷ mileage × fuel price + yearly upkeep ÷ 12
extra price(m) = extra price × (1 + rate ÷ 12)^m
EV unit price  = home share × home rate + (1 − home share) × public rate
page.methodology.solar.title: Rooftop solar
page.methodology.solar.body:
Each month, the tool works out your electricity bill twice through the state's slab tariff: once for your full use, and once for what is left after solar. Because the bill is worked out slab by slab, the units solar saves come off the most expensive slab first.

Units you export beyond your own use earn the export rate. The bill with solar never drops below the fixed charges. Panel output falls each year by the degradation rate, and the tariff rises once a year.

Payback is the first month the savings add up to the system's cost after subsidy. The return (IRR) is the yearly rate at which those savings exactly repay that cost.
page.methodology.solar.formula:
generation = kW × units per kW per day × 365 ÷ 12 × (1 − degradation)^(year − 1)
saving     = bill without solar − bill with solar
IRR        = (1 + monthly IRR)^12 − 1
page.methodology.rentBuy.title: Rent or buy
page.methodology.rentBuy.body:
The tool follows two households. The buyer pays the down payment, stamp duty and other purchase costs, then each month the EMI, maintenance on the home's value, and property tax that rises with inflation. The renter pays rent that rises once a year, and invests what the buyer spent at purchase, less the security deposit.

Each month, whoever pays less invests the difference at your return. At the end, each side's net worth is compared.
page.methodology.rentBuy.formula:
buyer net worth  = home value − loan still owed − cost of selling + buyer's investments
renter net worth = renter's investments + security deposit
page.methodology.limits.title: What the tools leave out
page.methodology.limits.body: Each tool lists the money factors it does not model, and a checklist of the things that are not about money. Where a value is not verified yet, the tool says so and asks you for your own figure instead of filling one in.

page.about.title: About CapitalVerdict
page.about.description: Why CapitalVerdict exists, who it is for, and how it is built.
page.about.intro: CapitalVerdict is a set of calculators for big money decisions in India: the kind that cost a lakh or more and that people usually make on a salesperson's numbers.
page.about.why.title: Why it exists
page.about.why.body: Most calculators show one confident answer and hide the assumptions behind it. A small change in fuel prices, rent or your return can flip that answer. CapitalVerdict shows every assumption, lets you change it, and tells you what would have to change for the other option to win.
page.about.how.title: How it works
page.about.how.body: Every tool runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere. The formulas are set out on the methodology page and checked against figures worked out by hand. Prices, rates and rules come from the sources listed on each tool and in the assumptions changelog.
page.about.contact.title: Found a mistake?
page.about.contact.body: Use the "Report an error" link at the bottom of any tool. Say which number looks wrong and why, and include a source if you have one.

prepay.metaDescription: Prepay your home loan or invest the money? Compare both with your own loan, amount and return: interest saved, how much sooner the loan ends, and the return at which investing wins.
prepay.explanation: The tool follows two households with the same money. One puts the amount into the loan and invests whatever that frees up each month: the whole EMI once the loan ends early, or the drop in EMI. The other invests the amount and keeps paying the loan as it is. Both spend the same each month. When the loan's original end date comes, neither owes anything, so the one with more invested is ahead.

prepay.faq.1.q: Why compare at the loan's original end date?
prepay.faq.1.a: By then both households owe nothing, so what each has invested is its whole position. Comparing earlier would mean weighing a smaller loan against a bigger investment pot, which hides the answer.
prepay.faq.2.q: Why does the return after tax matter so much?
prepay.faq.2.a: Prepaying earns exactly the loan rate, with no risk and no tax. Investing has to beat that after tax to come out ahead. The tool shows the return at which the two are level.
prepay.faq.3.q: Is the tax benefit on home-loan interest included?
prepay.faq.3.a: Only if you enter it. Whether you can deduct interest, and up to what limit, depends on your tax regime and the rules for the year, so the tool asks for your tax rate and the limit instead of assuming them. Prepaying lowers the interest, so it can lower this benefit too.
page.methodology.prepay.title: Prepay or invest
page.methodology.prepay.body:
The tool follows two households with the same money until the loan's original end date. One puts the amount into the loan; the other invests it. Both spend the original EMI's worth every month: whatever the loan does not take is invested at your return. With “keep the EMI”, the loan ends sooner and the whole EMI is invested afterwards; with “lower the EMI”, the EMI is recalculated over the same end date and the drop is invested.

A prepayment charge comes out of the amount paid in. If you enter a tax rate and a limit, the tax saved on each year's interest is invested at the year end, on both sides.
page.methodology.prepay.formula:
net worth = investments − loan still owed
answer    = prepay's net worth − invest's net worth at the original end date
cleared   = amount paid in ÷ (1 + prepayment charge)

carLoan.metaDescription: Pay cash for a car or take a loan? Compare both with your own price, loan rate and return: the EMI, the interest, and the return your savings need for the loan to pay off.
carLoan.explanation: The tool follows two buyers with the same money and the same car. The cash buyer pays the whole price today and then invests, every month, the EMI the other buyer pays. The loan buyer pays the down payment and the processing fee, invests the rest of the price, and pays the EMI. When the loan ends, both own the car and owe nothing, so the one with more invested is ahead.

carLoan.faq.1.q: Why does the cash buyer invest the EMI?
carLoan.faq.1.a: So both buyers spend the same each month. The loan buyer's EMI goes to the bank; the cash buyer, who has no EMI, puts the same amount into savings. Without that, the comparison would favour whoever spends less.
carLoan.faq.2.q: What is the loan's true cost?
carLoan.faq.2.a: The yearly rate at which what you actually receive (the loan less the processing fee) equals the EMIs you pay. A fee makes it higher than the quoted rate. Your savings have to earn more than this, after tax, for the loan to come out ahead.
carLoan.faq.3.q: Is the car's resale value included?
carLoan.faq.3.a: It does not need to be. Both buyers own the same car, so its value at the end is the same on both sides and cancels out. To compare petrol, CNG and electric cars, use the car fuel tool.
page.methodology.carLoan.title: Cash or car loan
page.methodology.carLoan.body:
The tool follows two buyers with the same money until the loan's last EMI. The cash buyer pays the whole price today and invests the EMI every month. The loan buyer pays the down payment and the processing fee, invests the rest of the price, and pays the EMI. Both own the same car at the end, so its value cancels out.

The return at which the two are level is the loan's true cost: the yearly rate that makes what you receive (loan less fee) equal to the EMIs you pay.
page.methodology.carLoan.formula:
cash buyer  = EMIs invested each month at your return
loan buyer  = (loan − fee) × (1 + return)^years
answer      = cash buyer − loan buyer
ac.metaDescription: Is a more efficient AC worth the extra price? Compare two ACs with their star-label units, your own use and your electricity rate: the yearly saving, the payback time and the use below which it never pays.
ac.explanation: The tool takes the units a year printed on each AC's star label and scales them by how much you run it compared with the label. In Delhi, it works out two real monthly bills, your other units plus each AC's, through the DERC tariff and the subsidy if you have opted in, and the difference is the saving. Elsewhere, the units you save times your price per unit is the saving. The saving rises once a year with the tariff. The extra price of the efficient AC is charged interest, as if borrowed or taken out of savings, and the answer is when the savings so far cover it.

ac.faq.1.q: Where do I find the units a year?
ac.faq.1.a: On the star label stuck on the AC and shown on the box and product page: the yearly energy figure in units (kWh). Use the same figure type for both ACs so they compare fairly.
ac.faq.2.q: My use is nothing like the label. What do I enter?
ac.faq.2.a: Your best guess compared with the label as a percentage. If you run it for only a few weeks of the year, enter less than 100%; if it runs most nights through a long summer, more. The “what would flip the answer” list shows the use below which the efficient AC never pays back.
ac.faq.3.q: Why count interest on the extra price?
ac.faq.3.a: Because the extra money is not free: you either borrow it or take it out of savings that would have earned something. Counting it makes the payback longer but honest. The payback ignoring interest is shown too.
page.methodology.ac.title: AC payback
page.methodology.ac.body: Each AC's units a year come from its star label, scaled by how much you run it compared with the label. The units saved, times your price per unit, is the saving, spread evenly over the months; the price per unit rises once a year. As in the car tool, the extra price is charged interest month by month, and the payback is the first month the savings so far cover it.
page.methodology.ac.formula:
units saved = (cheaper AC's units − efficient AC's units) × your use
saving      = units saved ÷ 12 × price per unit (rising yearly)
payback     = first month: savings so far ≥ extra price × (1 + r/12)^month
taxRegime.metaDescription: Old or new income-tax regime? Enter your salary and deductions to see the tax under each for 2026-27, worked out step by step, and the deductions the old regime needs to win.
taxRegime.explanation: The tool works out your tax twice, once under each regime, with the official slabs, standard deduction, rebate and 4% cess for the tax year. Under the new regime most deductions are not allowed, so only the standard deduction and any deductions you enter as allowed there are taken off. Under the old regime, your deductions and exemptions are taken off as you enter them. Whichever leaves less tax is better for you.

taxRegime.faq.1.q: What counts as deductions under the old regime?
taxRegime.faq.1.a: Everything you would claim beyond the standard deduction: the HRA exemption, tax-saving investments and insurance, health insurance, home-loan interest and similar. Choose “Item by item” and the tool holds each claim to its limit; or enter one total if you know it.
taxRegime.faq.2.a: Under the new regime, income up to the rebate limit pays no tax. Just above it, the tax would jump, so marginal relief caps the tax at the income above the limit. The tool applies it, as the official calculation does.
taxRegime.faq.3.q: What does the tool leave out?
taxRegime.faq.3.a: Surcharge on taxable income above ₹50 lakh, the higher exemption limits for people aged 60 and over, capital gains and other income taxed at special rates, and rounding to the nearest ten rupees. For those, use the Income Tax Department's own calculator or ask a tax professional.
page.methodology.taxRegime.title: Old or new tax regime
page.methodology.taxRegime.body: The tool works out the tax twice, with the slabs, standard deduction, rebate and cess for the tax year from the Income Tax Department. Taxable income is your salary and other income, less the standard deduction (up to your salary) and the deductions you enter for that regime. The rebate wipes out the tax up to its limit while taxable income is within the rebate's income limit. Under the new regime, marginal relief then caps the tax at the income above that limit. Cess is added on top.
page.methodology.taxRegime.formula:
taxable = salary + other income − standard deduction − your deductions
tax     = slab tax − rebate (or marginal relief, new regime)
total   = tax × (1 + 4% cess)

plotVs.metaDescription: Buying a plot, a fixed deposit or an equity mutual fund? Compare what each leaves you after stamp duty, selling costs and tax, with your own numbers, and see the price growth the plot needs to win.
plotVs.explanation: The tool takes what the plot really costs you today, price plus stamp duty, registration and other buying costs, and puts the same money in a fixed deposit and an equity mutual fund. After the years you choose, the plot is sold (less selling costs and capital-gains tax, with its yearly costs taken off), FD interest has been taxed every year at your rate, and the fund is sold with capital-gains tax above the yearly exemption. Whichever leaves you the most is ahead.
plotVs.scope: For resident individuals holding at least three years, so every gain is long-term. Tax rules are for 2026-27; exemptions for reinvesting plot gains are not included.

plotVs.faq.1.q: Why does the plot start behind?
plotVs.faq.1.a: Because stamp duty, registration and buying costs are spent on day one and earn nothing. The FD and the fund get that same money invested. The plot also costs money to sell and to hold, and pays no income while you own it.
plotVs.faq.2.q: How is the tax worked out?
plotVs.faq.2.a: Plot and fund gains held long enough are taxed at 12.5% plus cess when you sell; for the fund, the first ₹1.25 lakh of gains in that year is exempt, assuming you have no other equity gains that year. FD interest is taxed every year at your own rate. The rules and sources are in the table above.
plotVs.faq.3.q: What does the tool leave out?
plotVs.faq.3.a: Exemptions for reinvesting plot gains in a house or certain bonds, surcharge on high incomes, rent or crops from the plot, and fund costs beyond what the return you enter already reflects. If any of these apply to you, adjust the inputs or ask a tax professional.
page.methodology.plotVs.title: Plot vs FD vs mutual fund
page.methodology.plotVs.body: The tool starts with what the plot costs today, price plus stamp duty, registration and other buying costs, and invests the same amount in a fixed deposit and an equity mutual fund for the same years. The plot is sold at the end, less selling costs and long-term capital-gains tax on the gain over what was paid, and its yearly costs are subtracted as paid (without interest, which flatters the plot slightly). FD interest is taxed each year at your rate. The fund is taxed once, on the gain above the yearly exemption. Rates are from the Income Tax Department and PIB.

plot      = sale × (1 − selling cost) − 13% of gain − yearly costs × years
FD        = cash × (1 + rate × (1 − your tax rate))^years
fund      = value − 13% of (gain − ₹1.25 lakh)

fund.sip.faq.1.q: Why is this lower than other SIP calculators?
fund.sip.faq.1.a: Two reasons. We show what you keep after capital-gains tax, and we compound returns yearly, so 12% a year means 12% a year. Calculators that apply 1% a month end up a little higher, and most show the value before tax.
fund.sip.faq.2.q: How is a SIP taxed when I sell?
fund.sip.faq.2.a: Each instalment counts separately. Units held 12 months or less are short-term and taxed at 20%; the rest are long-term, with the first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term gains in a year tax-free and the rest taxed at 12.5%. Add 4% cess.
fund.sip.faq.3.a: A SIP that rises each year, for example by 10%, usually in step with your salary. Enter the yearly rise under "Filled in for you" to see the difference.
fund.lumpsum.faq.1.q: Lumpsum or SIP: which is better?
fund.lumpsum.faq.1.a: If returns are positive on average, money invested earlier has longer to grow, so a lump sum tends to end higher. A SIP spreads the risk of investing just before a fall. Many people with a lump sum move it in over a few months to split the difference.
fund.lumpsum.faq.2.a: Held more than 12 months, the gain is long-term: the first ₹1.25 lakh in a year is tax-free and the rest is taxed at 12.5%. Held 12 months or less, it is short-term and taxed at 20%. Add 4% cess.
fund.lumpsum.faq.3.a: An FD's interest is taxed every year at your slab rate, while a fund's gain is taxed once, when you sell. Comparing what each leaves after tax shows the real gap. Leave the FD rate empty to skip it.
fund.swp.faq.1.q: Is an SWP taxed like interest?
fund.swp.faq.1.a: No. Each withdrawal sells units, and only the gain in those units is taxed, as a capital gain. Early withdrawals are mostly your own money coming back, so the tax is usually low.
fund.swp.faq.2.q: How much can I withdraw safely?
fund.swp.faq.2.a: The answer card shows the most you can take for the years you choose, at the return you enter. A lower return or a few bad years early on shrink it, so many people take less than the maximum.
fund.swp.faq.3.q: Should the withdrawal rise each year?
fund.swp.faq.3.a: If the withdrawals pay your living costs, yes: prices rise, so a fixed amount buys less each year. Set the yearly rise to your expected inflation.
page.methodology.fund.title: SIP, lumpsum and SWP calculators
page.methodology.fund.body: One model runs all three. A lump sum is invested at the start, a SIP at the start of every month (raised each year by any step-up), and withdrawals are taken at the end of every month (raised each year if you choose). Every purchase is kept as its own lot, and withdrawals sell the oldest units first. Gains sold in each 12-month year of the plan are taxed under the equity rules: short-term if held 12 months or less, long-term above the yearly exemption, with cess. The SWP result is how long the withdrawals last and what is left; the most you can withdraw is found by trying amounts until the money just lasts.
page.methodology.fund.formula:
g      = (1 + yearly return)^(1/12) − 1
value  = Σ units held × (1 + g)^month
gain   = units sold × (price now − price when bought)
tax    = (short-term gain × 20% + (long-term gain − ₹1.25 lakh) × 12.5%) × 1.04, each year

page.methodology.planReturn.title: Plan return calculator
page.methodology.planReturn.body: Premiums are placed at the start of each month or year, and the plan's income and lump sums at the end of each month or year, on a monthly timeline. Tax, if any, is taken off everything paid back at one rate. The return is the internal rate of return of these cash flows: the monthly rate at which they net to zero, found by bisection and turned into a yearly rate. To compare with PPF, an FD or a fund, every payout is scaled by one factor so that, at that rate, the same premiums pay for them exactly.

real   = (1 + return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1

page.methodology.emi.title: EMI calculator
page.methodology.emi.body: The EMI is the level monthly payment that repays the loan over the tenure, with interest charged each month at the yearly rate divided by 12 on the balance still owed (reducing balance). The schedule is worked out month by month: interest on the opening balance, and the rest of the EMI repays the loan. A yearly prepayment is applied after every twelfth EMI and the EMI is kept, so the loan ends sooner. The last EMI in today's rupees divides it by inflation over the months to it.

page.methodology.termPlan.title: Term plus investing vs a plan
page.methodology.termPlan.body: The plan's premiums and payouts are placed on the same monthly timeline as in the plan return calculator. In the alternative, each plan premium goes into an investment when it would have been paid; the term premium is paid from it at the start of each cover year; and each payout the plan would make, after tax, is taken out of it. The investment grows at one return a year after tax, compounded monthly. If it runs below zero, the gap grows at the same rate. What is left at the end is the gain from term plus investing. The most a term plan can cost is that gain with free cover, divided by what one rupee of yearly premium would have grown to. The tie return is the rate at which the investment ends at exactly zero.

i           = (1 + return)^(1/12) − 1
most term   = left with free cover ÷ Σ (1 + i)^(N − 12k)
tie         = rate at which balance(N) = 0

debt.explanation: Every debt keeps its regular payment. Each month, interest is added to each debt at its yearly rate ÷ 12, the regular payments are made, and your spare money goes to the first debt in the order that is still owed. When a debt is cleared, its payment joins the spare money for the next one. The tool tries three orders: highest rate first, smallest balance first and lowest rate first. It compares them with paying only the regular payments.

debt.faq.1.a: Each rupee of spare money stops the interest on the rupee it repays. A rupee off a card at 36% stops more interest than a rupee off a home loan at 9%, so the highest rate first costs the least in total.
debt.faq.2.q: Why does the tool show smallest balance first?
debt.faq.2.a: Clearing a small debt quickly frees its payment and gives one less bill to track, which helps some people keep going. The tool shows what that costs in interest compared with the highest rate first, which is often little.
debt.faq.3.q: How is the credit card's interest worked out?
debt.faq.3.a: The same way as a loan's: the yearly rate ÷ 12 on what is carried over, each month. Cards charge interest on daily balances and can charge it on new spending too, so the real cost of carrying a balance is often higher.
page.methodology.debtOrder.title: Which debt to pay off first
page.methodology.debtOrder.body: Each month, interest is added to every debt at its yearly rate ÷ 12 on its balance, and its regular payment is made, or the whole balance if that is less. The spare money then goes to the first debt in the chosen order that is still owed, and any left over to the next. When a debt is cleared, its regular payment joins the spare money from the next month, and any part of it not needed in the month it clears goes to the next debt at once. A one-off amount today goes to the debts in the same order before the first month. Three orders are compared: highest rate first, smallest balance first and lowest rate first, against regular payments only. A run stops at 50 years; debts still owed then are shown as never cleared.

spare      = extra + payments of cleared debts

scooter.faq.1.q: Why work out charging from my whole bill?
scooter.faq.1.a: Because a unit's price depends on how many you already use. In Delhi, the first 200 units are free for homes that take the subsidy and the next 200 are half price. A scooter's 25 units can cost very little, or, if they push your home past 200, cost you the subsidy on the whole bill.
scooter.faq.2.a: Yes, through the price. The PM E-DRIVE incentive is taken off at the dealer, so the on-road price you enter already includes it. Delhi's own incentive is paid after registration, so the tool takes it off for you.
scooter.faq.3.a: Resale, insurance differences, parking and public charging. Add servicing and a battery replacement in the running costs if you expect them.
page.methodology.scooter.title: Electric or petrol scooter
page.methodology.scooter.body: Petrol costs distance ÷ mileage × the petrol price each month. The e-scooter draws distance ÷ km per unit from the wall; where the state's tariff is verified, those units cost the difference between the home's bill with and without them, slabs, levies and the bill subsidy included. That cost per unit then rises with the tariff each year, as petrol does with its own rise. The e-scooter's on-road price already has the central incentive taken off; the state incentive (by battery size, this year's rate and cap) and any scrapping bonus come off it at the start. The monthly savings are set against the extra price, charged interest monthly, as in the car fuel tool.
page.methodology.scooter.formula:
petrol     = km ÷ km/L × ₹/L
charging   = bill(other + km ÷ km/unit) − bill(other)
extra      = e-scooter − state incentive − scrapping − petrol scooter
net(month) = Σ (petrol − charging) − extra × (1 + r/12)^month
